items.stem: A 40-engineer healthcare platform's test-only convention began leaking into application code after a recent directory reorganization, though the model version is unchanged. Separately, a security rule for one command must hold on every call regardless of prompt wording. Select two configurations satisfying both requirements.

opts.t: A `.claude/rules/` entry scoped by a glob for the test directories, so the convention loads only for matching paths.
A `deny` rule for that command in `settings.json` permissions, enforced by Claude Code regardless of any prompt.
A firm instruction added to the skill body telling it never to touch application code or run that command.
Scope `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to exclude application-code paths and that command.

items.whyRight: The convention's leak into application code and the security rule's need to hold unconditionally are two separate gaps: a `.claude/rules/` glob confines the convention to matching test paths, and a `deny` rule enforces the security rule regardless of any prompt. Neither substitutes for the other.

whyWrong.C: A firm instruction in the skill body competes with everything else in context and can be missed on any run, unlike a rules-file glob or a deny rule.
whyWrong.D: `allowed-tools` governs which tools the skill may touch; it does not scope a convention to matching paths or make a rule hold regardless of what a prompt says.

items.t1Clause: a security rule for one command must hold on every call regardless of prompt wording

items.stem: A fintech startup's new payment-gateway integration must follow the gateway's fixed authentication rules, but three valid ways exist to receive transaction updates, each with different infrastructure cost, pending the compliance lead's approval. Which approach should the team take?

opts.t: Start implementing the polling approach directly, and switch to plan mode only if it proves too costly to maintain.
Adopt a standing rule that every integration in the codebase goes through plan mode and written approval, single-endpoint fixes included.
Treat the integration as fully spec-determined and implement directly, since the gateway's documentation fixes the required behavior.
Use plan mode to explore the three transaction-update approaches and present a design for approval before implementing.

items.whyRight: The transaction-update mechanism is not fixed by the gateway's documentation — three valid approaches remain, each carrying a different infrastructure cost — so the approach itself is still the decision being made. Plan mode explores that decision and produces a design the compliance lead can approve before implementation begins.

whyWrong.A: Starting with polling and switching to plan mode later means structural choices are already made before any deliberation, and reactive switching after implementation is underway costs more than planning upfront.
whyWrong.B: A blanket rule requiring plan mode and written approval for every integration, single-endpoint fixes included, taxes routine changes to control a risk that exists only here.
whyWrong.C: The stem states three valid ways exist to receive transaction updates, so the documentation does not fix the required behavior; treating it as spec-determined contradicts that stated fact.

items.t1Clause: but three valid ways exist to receive transaction updates

items.stem: A regulated payments firm's monorepo has teams whose own settings occasionally include a narrower allow rule for a dangerous command; the org's deny must still win. The restriction must also survive a developer editing their own local settings. Select two configurations.

opts.t: A hook that logs every attempt to run the command, for the team to review any bypass afterward.
A stronger, more explicit prohibition of the command restated across every project CLAUDE.md file the teams maintain.
A `deny` rule for the pattern — a matching deny wins over a matching allow regardless of specificity.
Managed enterprise policy settings, since nothing below it in the precedence order can be overridden locally.

items.whyRight: Two independent facts guarantee both requirements: a matching `deny` always wins over a matching `allow` regardless of specificity, and managed enterprise policy sits above every local settings file in precedence, so nothing a developer edits locally can override it. Either gap alone leaves the restriction incomplete.

whyWrong.A: A logging hook records that the command ran; it does not stop it, and answers neither the specificity question nor the local-override question.
whyWrong.B: Restating the prohibition more forcefully in CLAUDE.md shapes what Claude tries to do; it does not change what Claude Code allows, and prose holds no precedence tier at all.

items.t1Clause: the org's deny must still win

items.stem: A compliance-audit skill scans hundreds of configuration files for a specific historical vulnerability pattern before writing its final report, and the exploration step is consistently crowding the report itself out of context. The model version has not changed. What should change?

opts.t: Move to a more capable model with a larger context window, since the historical-pattern search is inherently complex.
Set `context: fork` so the exploration step runs in an isolated subagent context and only its result returns.
Add an instruction to the skill telling it to keep its exploration notes brief before drafting the report.
Scope `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to remove the tool it does not need for this task.

items.whyRight: The skill's exploration step is what floods context before the report can be written, and `context: fork` runs that step in an isolated subagent context so only its result returns to the main task. Neither the model nor the skill's tool list caused this pollution.

whyWrong.A: The model version has not changed, and a larger window does not remove the exploration output already filling it; this is a missing configuration boundary, not a capability limit.
whyWrong.C: Asking the skill to keep its notes brief asks the model to simulate isolation through instruction alone, competing with everything else in context instead of actually imposing a boundary.
whyWrong.D: Removing an unneeded tool governs what the skill may touch, not how much exploration output the model produces before the report; the crowding continues even with a narrower tool list.

items.t1Clause: is consistently crowding the report itself out of context

notes: g60/g62 keep their assigned facet IDs (F-7.2-02, F-7.8-02) per the brief's field instruction, but the correct pair's substantive content is built from two OTHER rows in the same section's decision table, as directed for these two slots: g60 from F-7.2-05 (.claude/rules glob for test-scoped conventions) + F-7.2-09 (deterministic hook/deny enforcement); g62 from F-7.8-06 (deny beats allow regardless of specificity) + F-7.8-07 (managed policy survives every local override). Both rows were confirmed unused in Papers 1-2. The assigned facet's own content (rejecting prose-in-skill-body / prose-in-CLAUDE.md as a substitute for the real mechanism) was folded in instead as the REPAIR distractor in each item, so the assigned facet is still directly represented.

g61 uses shape S5 ('rung selection on a ladder') applied to section 7.3 by framing the requirement as partly enumerable (the gateway's fixed authentication rules) and partly genuinely open (three valid transaction-update approaches) — S5's under-engineering direction. Prior papers only paired 7.3 with S3; flagging this pairing for the audit to double-check the fit, though no substitution was made since it holds up.

REPAIR is the best-fitting family for three of this sub-batch's eight distractor slots (g60-C, g62-B, g63-C) — each is a genuine 'prose beside the mechanism instead of the mechanism itself' case, directly grounded in corpus rows F-7.2-02, F-7.8-02, and F-7.2-04 respectively. Flagging the local concentration for the paper-wide balance pass, since it wasn't deliberately diversified within this batch.
